extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, researchers, and policy-makers interested in disinformation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize conceptual definitions, analytic frameworks, tactics, stages, and policy/research recommendations for identifying, studying, and responding to disinformation. Includes glossary-like entries for common techniques and evaluative dimensions used in research and policy discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: False or misleading information deliberately spread to deceive people, or to secure economic or political gain and which may cause public harm; an orchestrated adversarial activity employing strategic deceptions and media manipulation tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes intentionality (deliberate spread) and potential public harm; includes not only outright falsehoods but also truths, half-truths, and value judgements used strategically. Use this as the baseline criterion to classify content as disinformation rather than error or satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: disinformation vs misinformation vs malinformation (DMMI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-way distinction scholars agree on: (1) disinformation = strategic dissemination of false information with intent to cause public harm; (2) misinformation = unintentional spread of false information; (3) malinformation = factual information disseminated with the intention to cause harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent and truth-value/harm are the key axes. When evaluating material, assess whether falsehood is intentional (disinformation), accidental (misinformation), or factual but weaponized (malinformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: ABC framework (Actors, Behavior, Content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Camille François's 'ABC' framework: Manipulative Actors (those engaging knowingly and covertly), Deceptive Behavior (techniques to enhance reach/virality), and Harmful Content (types of damaging messages such as health misinformation, manipulated media, harassment, violent extremism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three components as analytical dimensions: identify actors (who), catalogue behaviors/tactics used (how), and evaluate the content's harms (what). Examples: troll farms (behavior), state media personas (actors), deepfakes (content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution, Degree and Effect (additional analytic dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brookings proposed 'Distribution' (technical protocols shaping behavior); Carnegie suggested adding 'Degree' (how widely content is distributed and who it reaches) and 'Effect' (how much threat or harm a given case poses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing cases, measure not just content and intent but distribution channels, audience size/composition, and observed/likely effects on public opinion, behavior, or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeding vs Echoing (two-stage spread model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation spread on social media can be classified into two stages: 'seeding' (malicious actors strategically insert deceptions into an ecosystem) and 'echoing' (audiences disseminate disinformation as their own opinions, often incorporated into confrontational fantasies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether content is being injected by coordinated actors (seeding) or amplified organically/argumentatively by audiences (echoing). Countermeasures may differ by stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main methods of seeding disinformation online
rubrics_metrics.description: Four main seeding methods identified: selective censorship, manipulation of search rankings, hacking and releasing (leaks/forged materials), and directly sharing disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of detection/evaluation check for evidence of search-rank manipulation, engineered leaks/forgeries, suppression of corrective information, or direct placement and amplification strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and social media manipulation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of online digital technologies—including algorithms, social bots, automated scripts—for commercial, social, military, or political purposes to steer public opinion, polarize citizens, circulate conspiracies, or silence dissidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include abnormal bot-like activity, rapid repeated posting, coordinated timing across accounts, and algorithmic gaming. Consider both technical and social-protocol vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploiting online advertising technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification of disinformation via online advertising malpractice, especially real-time bidding (machine-to-machine interactions), monetization incentives, and use of dark money for political advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review ad supply-chain evidence, funding sources, targeting parameters, and whether programmatic ad systems were used to boost reach or monetize fabricated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astroturfing
rubrics_metrics.description: A centrally coordinated campaign that mimics grassroots activism by making participants pretend to be ordinary citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for signs of coordination, repeated messaging across accounts with similar language/timing, and inauthentic accounts posing as local activists or ordinary users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clickbait
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate use of misleading headlines and thumbnails to increase online traffic for profit or popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate headline-content mismatch, sensationalized framing, and referral paths designed to maximize clicks rather than inform; often used to monetize disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda (organized mass communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized mass communication with a hidden agenda and a mission to conform belief and action by circumventing individual reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether messaging is part of coordinated, sustained campaigns designed to shape beliefs and behavior rather than present balanced information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspiracy theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttals of official accounts that propose alternative explanations in which individuals or groups act in secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidentiary basis, reliance on hidden-cause narratives, and tendency to incorporate unverifiable claims that resist falsification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudoscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts that claim the explanatory power of science, borrow its language and legitimacy but diverge substantially from its quality criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for misuse of scientific language, lack of peer review, absence of replicable methods, and cherry-picking of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoax / Fake news (genre vs label)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoax: news presenting false facts as legitimate. 'Fake news' as a genre describes deliberate pseudo-journalism; as a label it is often instrumentalized to delegitimize media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between intentionally fabricated stories and mislabeling of legitimate reporting; beware of the term 'fake news' being used as a political weapon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Echo chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: An epistemic environment in which participants encounter beliefs and opinions that coincide with their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure homogeneity of information sources, algorithmic personalization effects, and network clustering that limits exposure to corrective information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive behavior: trolling, paid engagement, bots
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques viral deception actors use to enhance reach and impact, including troll farms, internet bots, astroturfing, and paid engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect unnatural engagement patterns, sudden spikes from coordinated clusters, use of sockpuppet accounts, and paid amplification networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of forged documents and fabricated intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of forged documents, manuscripts, and photographs or fabricated intelligence to mislead audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticate provenance, verify metadata and corroboration, and treat single-source 'leaks' with heightened suspicion unless independently validated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front groups and disguised actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations or accounts that hide true objectives or controllers to mislead the public about motives and origins of messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace funding, board/leadership links, and coordination signals; transparency of sponsorship and declared motives reduces likelihood of front-group manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical test for disinformation in warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical/ethical test: whether disinformation was performed out of a motivation of good faith and acceptable according to the rules of war; some uses may be permissible (e.g., inflatable decoys), others not (e.g., disguising a munitions plant as a healthcare facility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating information operations in conflict, weigh intentions, proportionality, and whether the tactic violates protections for civilians or humanitarian norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of societal impact (trust, polarization, democratic erosion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects used to evaluate seriousness: undermining public trust, fragmenting the factual basis for debate, contributing to political polarization and democratic erosion or regime resilience in authoritarian contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess shifts in public trust metrics, polarization indicators, incidence of violence or civic disruption following campaigns, and institutional resilience to information attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research & policy response recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly guidance to move beyond fact-checking and media literacy toward systemic, multidisciplinary, and market-oriented approaches; include analysis of business models, cultural contexts, and gendered-based disinformation; emphasize global (not Anglocentric) perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate counter-disinformation programs on whether they address underlying market incentives, platform architectures, cross-cultural differences, and structural causes rather than only surface-level fact correction.
